title: The ancestors
hook: some Chinese homes keep an altar for the ancestors

segments.voice: Yesterday, Confucian self-cultivation: the Great Learning's chain, with the self as the root. Your line was start with me. Which small thing did you put in order? Day one thousand four hundred nine.

On a high shelf in a family's living room there's a small altar. Wooden tablets stand on it, each carved or painted with a name. A grandfather. A great-grandmother. Names going back further than anyone in the room has met. In front of them, a dish of oranges, a cup of tea, a little bowl of sand with incense sticks standing in it. In the morning someone lights a stick, bows, and says a few words. On a birthday, a favorite dish appears on the shelf before anyone else eats. In some Chinese homes, this shelf is where the family keeps company with the people it came from. Today, the ancestors.
screen: `A SMALL ALTAR, A ROW OF NAMES.` → `ORANGES, TEA, INCENSE.` → `KEEPING COMPANY WITH THE DEAD.`

segments.voice: Tradition says honoring the ancestors is older than Confucius. What the Analects shows is his attention to how it's done. The Analects says of him, in Legge's translation: "He sacrificed to the dead, as if they were present." As if they were present. That small phrase carries a lot. It doesn't settle what happens to the dead. It doesn't argue. It describes a way of standing in front of them: with full attention, the way you'd stand if a grandmother walked into the room. Some readers hear in it a belief that the ancestors are really there. Others hear an attitude of reverence that matters whether or not they are. Families can hold both. Another passage, in paraphrase, says that when people take care with the funeral rites of their parents, and keep remembering them long after, the goodness of the whole people grows full again. So the altar isn't only about the dead. It shapes the living. A child who watches her father bow to a name learns that she, too, belongs to a line, that she owes something to people she never met, and that someday she'll be the name on the shelf. Then there are the seasonal days. At the spring festival of Qingming, families go out to the graves, sweep them clean, pull the weeds, and leave food and flowers. Tomb sweeping is real work, done with brooms, and it ends in a meal. Under all of it is a simple idea. Nobody starts from nothing. Every one of us is standing on a long line of people who carried life this far, and remembering them is a way of saying so out loud.
screen: `AS IF THEY WERE PRESENT.` · `A BELIEF, OR A WAY OF STANDING?` · `THE ALTAR SHAPES THE LIVING.` · `QINGMING: SWEEPING THE GRAVES.` · then, large: `HE SACRIFICED TO THE DEAD, AS IF THEY WERE PRESENT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: honor one ancestor. Settle, and breathe. Let one person who came before you step forward. A grandparent, a great-aunt, a parent who has died. If your family history is hard, or unknown, choose someone whose life made yours possible in another way, or simply the unnamed people who carried your line this far. Say their name inside, if you know it. Stand before them, in your mind, as if they were present. What would you want to tell them? If you pray, you can remember them in your prayer. The bell holds the time.
The ancestors. Those who came before, honored in Chinese tradition at home altars and at the graves, with attention, as if they were present. Today's word.
Your line: the ancestors. Today, do one small thing in someone's memory: cook their dish, tell their story to someone, look at a photo for a full minute. Day one thousand four hundred nine.

howItsDone: Families who keep Chinese ancestral customs light incense and offer food and tea before tablets bearing the names of their dead, and at Qingming in spring they visit the graves to sweep them, make offerings, and share a meal.

fork.setup: you're at a family altar for the first time and unsure whether the ancestors are really there. by the Analects, how do you stand before them?
options: only bow if you're sure they're present.
stand as if they were present.
skip it until you've decided what you believe.
fork.reveal: Confucius "sacrificed to the dead, as if they were present": full attention, without settling the question first.

trapdoor: what you thought: ancestor altars are about worshiping the dead.
what it means: keeping company with those who came before, with attention, as if they were present, and learning you belong to a line.
what a scholar hears: Analects 3.12's "as if present" leaves open whether the dead are there; readers have heard both belief and reverent attitude.

sources.quoted: He sacrificed to the dead, as if they were present.

notes: Analects 3.12 quoted from Legge 1861 from memory; verify exact wording. Analects 1.9 (Zengzi on care with funeral rites and remembering the long departed) is paraphrased and attributed only to 'another passage'.
The index hook says 'many Chinese homes'; under the claims rule the script and its hook field say 'some Chinese homes' and give no number. The index line is left unchanged.
'Honoring the ancestors is older than Confucius' is a historical claim without a date; cut or soften if the editor prefers ('tradition says').
Qingming described as a spring festival of tomb sweeping, with no date. Confirm.
Altar details (tablets, oranges, tea, incense, a favorite dish on a birthday) are illustrative of one family, not claims about all homes.
Practice offers a path for listeners with hard or unknown family histories.
